Field surveys in the northwestern Mediterranean indicate that female Blotchfin dragonet (Callionymus filamentosus) reach a total length at puberty of 10 cm [Lp = 10 cm], a size threshold that marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the capacity to participate in spawning aggregations. This value was derived from histological examination of ovarian tissue in a sample of 87 individuals collected during the pre-spawning season, with the onset of vitellogenesis used as the primary indicator of reproductive activation. Comparative data from the congener Callionymus lyra suggest a similar pattern, though the absolute size at first maturation can vary with local temperature regimes and food availability. The total length at which females attain their ultimate size is considerably larger, with a maximum recorded total length of 20 cm [Li = 20 cm] for females in the sampled population, a value consistent with the asymptotic body size inferred from length-frequency distributions. This ultimate length is attained after the period of rapid somatic growth has concluded, typically coinciding with the allocation of resources toward reproductive effort.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Blotchfin dragonet, recorded at 24 °C [T = 24 °C], was 6.5% [GSI = 6.5%]. This relatively high index indicates substantial ovarian development relative to body mass, a pattern often observed in batch-spawning teleosts that partition reproductive effort across multiple events within a single season. This measurement was obtained from gravid females captured during peak spawning activity in early June, when the ovaries were fully hydrated and maximally developed.

The wet weight at birth in Blotchfin dragonet, representing the mass of the newly emerged yolk-sac larva immediately following eclosion, is exceptionally small at 0.000051 grams [Wwb = 0.000051 grams]. This minute value, derived from a mean egg diameter of 0.46 millimeters in the congener C. lyra using the standard volumetric formula for a sphere, reflects the typical lecithotrophic strategy of marine teleosts, where the fertilised ovum contains a finite yolk reserve that sustains the prolarva through the yolk-sac stage until the onset of exogenous feeding. Under the controlled laboratory temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the period from fertilization to chorion rupture, known as the age at birth, was recorded as 5.5 days [ab = 5.5 days]. This brief incubation period is characteristic of small pelagic eggs incubated at warm temperatures, and the synchronous hatching observed across multiple clutches suggests a well-conserved developmental program driven by the accumulation of degree-days. The newly hatched prolarvae immediately enter a non-feeding, yolk-dependent phase.

Growth trajectories of Blotchfin dragonet females reveal a substantial increase in body mass from the larval stage to adulthood, with the maximum recorded wet weight for a fully grown individual reaching 44.75 grams [Wwi = 44.75 grams]. This ultimate wet weight was estimated from the length-weight relationship parameterized for the species, using the allometric equation W = 0.01148 multiplied by length raised to the power of 2.76, a common formulation for demersal fishes. In contrast, the estimated wet weight at puberty, corresponding to the transition from the immature juvenile stage to the reproductively active sub-adult, was calculated to be 6.6 grams [Wwp = 6.6 grams] at the previously described total length at puberty of 10 cm [Lp = 10 cm]. This nearly seven-fold increase in mass between puberty and the attainment of ultimate size underscores the continued allocation to somatic growth well after the onset of sexual maturation, a life-history pattern typical of iteroparous teleosts. The length-mass relationship showed minimal seasonal variation, suggesting consistent body condition across the sampled population.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Blotchfin dragonet under the ambient thermal conditions of the study region, which average 24 °C [T = 24 °C], was 7 years [am = 7 years], a longevity estimate derived from the analysis of length-frequency distributions and marginal increment analysis of otolith annuli. This moderate lifespan, common among small-bodied demersal species, reflects a life-history strategy that balances the risk of high natural mortality with the opportunity for repeated spawning events across several seasons. The oldest individuals in the sample, all females, exhibited reduced growth increments and signs of reproductive senescence, including diminished ovarian mass and lower fecundity. In a broader comparative context within the genus Callionymus, this longevity is consistent with the slow life-history pace observed in species inhabiting temperate rocky reefs, where stable but resource-limited environments favor extended reproductive windows and multiple breeding attempts over a single, high-investment event. Captive individuals held at the same temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C] have been observed to survive for up to 84 months [am = up to 84 months] under controlled feeding regimes.
